Courtesy: CSU Archives / Everett Collection Historical / Alamy In 1936, the Black American anthropologist Eslanda Robeson embarked on a three-month journey to Africa. Partly organised by the British Government, a file at The National Archives reveals her personal reflections of the trip and the profound impact it had on her. Author Sarah Castagnetti Roles Author Visual Collections Specialist On this page 'I have roots' Marriage to Paul Robeson Journey planning Colonial Office motivations African Journey Problems with Customs Lasting impact Important information ! This article features quotes from a document and a book which include outdated language to describe Black people. 'I have roots' I feel now that at least I have roots, that there are millions of other people like me. Eslanda Robeson, Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 This powerful sentence was written by Eslanda (Essie) Goode Robeson (1895–1965) following a three-month journey through Africa in 1936. Essie was writing to Hanns Vischer, Joint Secretary to the Advisory Committee on Education in the Colonies for Britain, who had helped arrange her travels. From her letter, the impact of her experiences is palpable. Open transcript 19 Buckingham Street Adelphi, London. Sunday, 18 October. My dear Major Vischer, Well, we're back safe and sound. I wasn't so sound when I first returned. I'd got some germ, which lodged in my intestinal wall, and gave me a dreadful time. But my small son was very fit, and actually took care of me during the last lap of the journey. We had a marvellous time. In many ways. You know, all Americans, except Negroes, come from somewhere, - Italy, Germany, England etc. All have, way back, a “mother” Country. But we Negroes have none. This visit to Africa made me feel very much the way I'm sure a German American must feel when he first visits his “Old Country". I feel now that at least I have roots, that there are millions of other people like me - black and all shades of brown, - and so I feel more comfortable generally. If you know what I mean. It was even more important for my son. He now knows there are millions of black people, and that he is by no means a freak of nature, with his brown skin!!! But of course there were many many interesting things and people. Some day, if I may, I'll come in and tell you about some of them, and show you my films and snapshots. Eslanda Robeson's letter to Hanns Vischer at the Colonial Office, 18 October 1936. Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 You know, all Americans, except Negroes, come from somewhere, – Italy, Germany, England etc. All have, way back, a “mother” Country. But we Negroes have none. This visit to Africa made me feel very much the way I'm sure a German American must feel when he first visits his “Old Country". I feel now that at least I have roots, that there are millions of other people like me. Eslanda Robeson, Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 Essie’s words illustrate the profound impression her experiences made on her – a Black American woman living in the first part of the 20th century. But who was Essie and why was the Colonial Office helping her? Marriage to Paul Robeson Essie was best known for being married to Paul Robeson, the internationally famous Black American singer, actor and political activist. The pair met at Colombia University and married in 1921. Essie graduated in chemistry and was the first Black person to head the surgical pathology and histological chemistry department at New York City's Presbyterian Hospital. In 1925, as Paul’s career took off, Essie left her job to become his manager. In 1928 they moved to London with their baby son, Paul Junior (Pauli). They had originally gone to the capital so Paul could appear in Show Boat at the Drury Lane Theatre. Following the run, however, they decided to stay and moved to Hampstead in the northwest of the city. Paul and Eslanda Robeson sitting with their son, Paul Jr, outside their house in Enfield, Connecticut, USA, 1940s. Courtesy: CSU Archives / Everett Collection Historical / Alamy In 1934 Essie began studying anthropology at the London School of Economics (LSE). In her 1946 book, ‘African Journey’ she relates her frustration at the academic perception of African people as 'primitive', and the dismissiveness she encountered when she put forward her own views: I soon became fed up with white students and teachers “interpreting” the Negro mind and character to me. Especially when I felt, as I did very often, that their interpretation was wrong. It went something like this: Me, I am Negro, I know what we think, how we feel… “Ah, no, my dear, you’re wrong. You see you are European. You can’t possibly know how the primitive mind works until you study it, as we have done… You’ve never been out there, you’ve never seen them and talked with them on their home ground; you can’t possibly know” Eslanda Robeson, African Journey, 1946 To Essie, these attitudes were nothing new. They reminded her of arguments she had heard in the United States. Journey planning It was in 1936, eight years after their arrival in London, that Essie embarked on her first trip to Africa. She had a long-held ambition to visit the continent, and her experiences at LSE, along with a desire to connect 8-year-old Pauli to African cultures appear to have given her the push she needed. Having lived in the UK from the age of 10 months, Essie commented that Pauli 'had thought we were the only brown people in a totally white world.' Essie planned to visit Cape Province and Johannesburg in South Africa, followed by Swaziland (now Eswatini), Mozambique and Uganda where she would carry out her anthropological fieldwork with herdspeople – traditional nomadic communities – in Toro. Initially, there were difficulties in obtaining visas. Essie wrote in African Journey: It seems if you are Negro, you can’t make up your mind to go to Africa, and just go. Oh no. Not unless you are a missionary. The white people in Africa do not want educated Negroes traveling around seeing how their brothers live; nor do they want those brothers seeing Negroes from other parts of the world, hearing how they live. Eslanda Robeson, African Journey, 1946 Essie had to provide the Colonial Office with evidence that she was studying at LSE and the trip was for her fieldwork, before the visas were issued. Colonial Office motivations A Colonial Office file in the collections here at The National Archives provides insight into the concerns and motivations of the Colonial Office in assisting Essie with her trip. After receiving a request from Essie’s professor, Bronislaw Malinowski, to give all possible assistance, a Colonial Office memo, written by a Mr Flood, notes that: For many reasons it is rather advisable that Mrs Robeson should be treated as decently as may be possible... you can readily realise that colour prejudice may arise. (She ought to be used to that in the States, however.) But, as you know, [Paul] Robeson is rather a figure in the world... No doubt you can arrange for whatever facilities may be possible to be given to Mrs Robeson, as if she were one of the white ‘researcher workers’ who appear from time to time. J E W Flood, Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 Open transcript DOWNING STREET. 26 May, 1936. AIR MAIL CONFIDENTIAL Dear Merrick, This is about the rummiest letter I have ever written to you. Mrs. Paul Robeson, wife of the great Paul Robeson, is busy planning a visit to East Africa. She has been over here for some years and has attended courses and instruction under Professor Malinowski at the London School of Economics (she would!). She has been anxious for some years to get out to Africa so as to see something of the African people and this summer she has arranged her husband’s work so that she can leave him. She proposes to go out to Nyasaland and there stay with Miss Margaret Read, who is carrying out research Colonial Office memo written by J E W Flood on Essie Robeson's proposed trip. Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 Hanns Vischer appears to have taken responsibility for arranging the assistance requested by Professor Malinowski. Vischer wrote letters of introduction for Essie connecting her to people in Africa who he felt could be helpful to her. He sent separate covering letters to the same contacts, expressing a desire to ensure the work of the Colonial Office was shown in a positive light: Most of what she knows about Africa she has learnt at the London School of Economics, where extreme and one-sided views are very much in vogue. She is a delightful woman and I think, in spite of all she heard, quite open-minded. She has a great influence on her husband who, as you know, is looked up to by all coloured people in this country. So please do what you can to help in giving her a fair idea of our African problems and the work our various Governments are doing to solve them. Hanns Vischer, Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 The Colonial Office’s willingness to assist Essie appears to have been based on more than academic goodwill. The correspondence reveals concerns about reputation, international politics and the exposure of colonial rule to someone who had the potential to publicly challenge it. By Spring 1936, Essie’s plans were in place, and first-class passage was booked for her and Pauli on the SS Winchester Castle which sailed from Southampton on 29 May. The Board of Trade passenger list , which details those who set sail from Ireland or Britain during the 19th and 20th centuries, shows their entry under the list of ‘alien’ passengers. The entry is written as ‘Robeson (Mrs Paul) Eslanda Goode’ (age 39) and ‘Master Paul’ (age 8). Essie is described as a student and her address is given as 19 Buckingham Street, Strand, London. Open transcript Name of Ship: Winchester Castle Date of Departure: 29th May 1936 Where Bound: South Africa Name and Descriptions of Alien Passengers Embarked at the Port of Southampton Names of Passengers: Robeson (Mrs Paul) Eslanda Goode, Master Paul Last Address in the United Kingdom: 19 Buckingham Street, Strand, London Profession, Occupation, or Calling of Passenger: Student Ages of Passengers: 39, 8 Country of which Citizen or Subject: American Country of Intended Future Permanent Residence: England SS Winchester Castle passenger list, date of departure 29 May 1936. Catalogue reference: BT 27/1462 The Board of Trade passenger lists have numerous entries for Paul and Essie as they criss-crossed the Atlantic during the 1920s and 30s for Paul’s work. Until 1928 Essie’s occupation is given as chemist, but after she gave up her job at the New York Presbyterian Hospital her entries begin listing her occupation as housewife. African Journey After traveling through South Africa and different destinations along the east coast, Essie and Pauli arrived at Toro in Uganda where she began her fieldwork, studying the herdspeople there. On 20 July Essie wrote to Hanns Vischer thanking him for his assistance and listing the places they had seen: Open transcript My dear Major Vischer, Pauli and I are having the most marvellous trip. We did 2000 miles by car thru South Africa, visiting Basutoland especially, attending a real African wedding, and an all-African convention at Bloemfontein. We ended up at Johannesburg where we saw the mines. Then down thru Portuguese East Africa to Lorenco Marques, where we caught the coast steamer. Called at Beira, Ibo, Dar Es Salaam and Zanzibar. Off the ship at Mombasa, by train up thru Kenya to Nairobi; saw Kilimanjaro at dawn, came thru the Game reserve, to Pauli’s great delight. Were collected at Kampala by our friend Nyabongo, who brought us to Toro. We are now installed in a Chief’s house here; a whole wing has been turned over to us, we have our own private courtyard, private bath enclosure, etc. We have discarded everything European and are living entirely African fashion, – eating with our hands and everything. Everyone is so interested in us, that they bring us presents from far and near, and sit and ask questions about the outside world. They are giving every every help with my field work, – in fact bringing everything which is trans-portable here so I can see and watch without going out in the heat. I think I shall be able to do a good piece of field work as a result. I want to thank you most earnestly and warmly for all the help you have given me. Everywhere officials have made my way clear and easy, have been beautifully hospitable, and intelligently helpful. I have not been able to see too much of them, because I have had to be entirely with Africans, in order to see their customs. I hope you have had a pleasant summer. I will drop in to see you in person, in order to thank you properly, when we return in early September. Sincerely, Eslanda Goode Robeson Mrs.Paul Robeson. Eslanda Robeson's letter to Hanns Vischer at the Colonial Office, 20 July 1936. Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 Pauli and I are having the most marvellous trip. We did 2000 miles by car thru South Africa, visiting Basutoland especially, attending a real African wedding, and an all-African convention at Bloemfontein. We ended up at Johannesburg where we saw the mines. Eslanda Robeson, Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 The next leg of their journey took them through East Africa: to Lorenco Marques, where we caught the coast steamer. Called at Beira, Ibo, Dar Es Salaam and Zanzibar. Off the ship at Mombasa, by train up thru Kenya to Nairobi; saw Kilimanjaro at dawn, came thru the Game reserve, to Pauli’s great delight. Were collected at Kampala by our friend Nyabongo, who brought us to Toro. Eslanda Robeson, Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 Essie’s trip is detailed in her engaging and revealing book, ‘African Journey’. Although it wasn’t published until 1946, it is based on diaries she kept during the 1936 journey. The book goes into detail about Essie’s reactions to the living and working conditions she witnessed in the places she visited, and it’s interesting that she doesn’t mention this in her letter to Vischer. It seems reasonable to conclude that she knew it would be too controversial. Problems with Customs Her fieldwork complete, Essie and Pauli began the arduous journey home by plane from Entebbe, in Uganda, to Alexandria, in Egypt (completed in stages over four days), then by seaplane to Brindisi in Italy, train to Paris and a final flight to London, arriving on 25 August. As Essie tells Vischer, on the return she came down with 'some germ' which gave her 'a dreadful time'. Fortunately, she writes that Pauli was able to take 'care of me during the last lap of the journey'. Their luggage was shipped separately, but when it arrived, UK Customs asked her to declare the value of the items she was bringing back. Essie wrote to Vischer for advice, explaining that the items were: specimens of bead, pottery, ebony and ivory work of the natives in south and central Africa. They are, of course, for my African Museum collection, and most certainly not for sale, nor for gifts. I have no idea how to evaluate them, as I dare say, commercially, they have very little value. Eslanda Robeson, Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 Open transcript CONTENTS OF 3 PACKAGES EX s.s. “GRANTULLY CASTLE”. No.1. Suit Case. Personal Clothing. Books & Private Papers. 1 Bead Necklet. X 1 Parcel Gramophone Records. X a present to Mrs. Robeson from Griffiths Motsieloa & The Singer Gramophone Coy. Johannesburg. 99 Different rolls of films. ? 84 photographic. ) X ? 11 cine films. ) German X No.2. Suit Case. Dozen Wicker Mats. X 2 “[wicker] Baskets. X 1 Wood Small Stand. X 1 Wood Carved Native’s Head (Man’s) X pair. 1 “[wood]“ [carved] (Woman’s) “[Native’s]“ [Head]… X 1 “[wood]“ Playing Tom-tom. X Personal Clothing. Books No.3. Trunk. 3 Metal Vases. X Personal Clothing. 1 Roll film, photographic. X Numerous Small Ivory Carvings. X Books. The items Eslanda Robeson declared to Customs on her return to the UK Catalogue reference: CO 822/70/14 In her book, Essie notes how in Africa, when she said she admired something, she later found she was presented with a gift: 'Africans, with their exquisite politeness, will give you things you admire'. These included 'lovely beadwork', 'a beautiful Swazi wedding headdress', 'Zulu pieces from Natal'. To Essie these were all 'priceless – a museum collection, and I would show it everywhere.' For Essie, the items represented knowledge, relationships and lived experience, and giving them a financial value was understandably difficult. Lasting impact Essie’s ‘African Adventure’ and her letter to Hanns Vischer in October 1936 show the profound impact her experiences in Africa had on her. Both she and Paul had been active advocates for civil rights in America, but after her journey, Essie’s understanding of the impact of colonialism on populations across the world was clarified. On 1 October 1939, following the start of the Second World War, the family left the UK and moved back to the US. In 1941 she and Paul joined the Council on African Affairs, an American organisation promoting Pan-Africanism and anti-colonialism. In 1946 she obtained a PhD in anthropology from Hartford Seminary in Connecticut and in the same year ‘African Journey’ was published. Essie and Paul were viewed with suspicion by the American authorities, and for many years in the 1950s their passports were revoked and they were unable to travel. Once their passports were returned in 1958, Essie attended the first post-colonial All-African Peoples’ Conference in Ghana. Essie died in New York in 1965, just before her 70th birthday. Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection The story of The Battle of Cable Street In 1936, Cable Street in London’s East End became the site of violent clashes between the British Union of Fascists and anti-fascist demonstrators. For many, this event symbolised community resistance to fascism, but what can archival records reveal about the realities behind this narrative? About this image Demonstrators at the junction of Aldgate and Commercial Road, from the Illustrated London News, 1936. On this page The road to Cable Street Opposition to the march 'They shall not pass' The aftermath of Cable Street Archives and collective memory Explore the records used in this story Important information ! This content discusses violence, antisemitism and discrimination. This material and related language is included to accurately reflect the past and the nature of our records. The road to Cable Street On Sunday 4 October 1936, a march through East London led by Oswald Mosley and the British Union of Fascists (BUF) was disrupted by anti-fascist counterdemonstrators. The BUF supported fascism, a far-right movement that believed some groups were superior to others. They also supported the use of violence against people who opposed their ideas. The BUF intended to parade through areas with significant Jewish populations but were stopped by a coalition of working men and women, Jewish people, dockers and immigrants. The Battle of Cable Street, as these events are often referred to, has developed an almost mythic status, representing the East End’s clear rejection of fascism. It is commemorated with a plaque and mural on walls along Cable Street. The Cable Street mural, found on St George’s Town Hall, Tower Hamlets. Photo taken by Simon Demissie. Records at The National Archives show a more nuanced picture. They indicate attempts to ban the fascist demonstration as well as advice from left wing and Jewish groups encouraging counterdemonstrators to avoid the march. Our records also show a spike in support for the BUF in East London in the immediate aftermath of The Battle of Cable Street. The BUF had developed a significant but notorious profile throughout the mid-1930s, even if it had failed to gather any electoral success, due to their extremist actions. For example, protestors at a BUF meeting in June 1934 were brutally beaten by the group. Additionally, street attacks on communists and Jewish people were committed regularly and continued until 1936. The BUF intended to celebrate this summer campaign on 4 October through a march and meetings in Shoreditch, Limehouse, Bow and Bethnal Green. Some of the group’s members openly declared that the march was a pogrom (targeted attack) on East London’s Jewish communities. Opposition to the march The upcoming march motivated action from the local community. In the week leading up to it a group of East End mayors firmly asked the Home Secretary Sir John Simon to ban it, with the Mayor of Stepney claiming that a march: …in this large Jewish populated area cannot but be provocative of disturbance and possible riot and danger to persons and property The Mayor of Stepney, 1936, Catalogue reference: HO 144/21060 Open transcript To THE RIGHT HON. SIR JOHN SIMON, P.C. H.M. Secretary for Home Affairs. WE, the undersigned citizens of East London, view with grave concern the proposed march of the British Union of Fascists upon East London. The avowed object of the Fascist movement in Great Britain is the incitement of malice and hatred against sections of the population. It aims to further ends which seek to destroy the harmony and goodwill which has existed for centuries among the East London population, irrespective of differences in race and creed. We consider racial incitement by a movement which employs flagrant distortion of truth and degrading calumny and vilification as a direct and deliberate provocation to malicious attack. We therefore make an earnest appeal to His Majesty's Secretary of State for Home Affairs, to prohibit such marches and thus retain peaceable and amicable relations between all sections of East London's population. Petition to Home Secretary Sir John Simon from Jewish residents of the East End. Catalogue reference: HO 144/21060 In the two days prior to the march the Jewish People’s Council collected an impressive 100,000 signatures to protest their ‘grave concern’. The petition expressed their fear that the ‘avowed object of the Fascist movement in Great Britain is the incitement of malice and hatred against sections of the population’. The petition ultimately asked the Home Secretary to prohibit such marches to unite and protect the community. Open transcript JEWISH PEOPLE’S COUNCIL AGAINST FASCISM AND ANTI-SEMITISM. NON POLITICAL 164 Commercial Road, E.1. 30th September 1936 The Right Hon. Sir John Simon, P.C. H.M. Secretary of State for Home Affairs. Dear Sir, The Jewish People’s Council is earnestly desirous for permission to have a deputation wait upon you in regard to the proposed British Union of Fascists march in East London on Sunday 4th October. As a large organisation with a specialised knowledge of conditions prevailing in East London at the moment (resultant upon recent Fascist agitation in the Area), we are most anxious to assist the Authorities in maintaining peace and order. We propose that our deputation be received by you on Friday, 2nd prox. at 11.30 a.m. when a petition supported by 100,000 signatures obtained within 2 days, expressing the feelings of East London’s population in the matter of the proposed march, will be presented. The deputation is in the position to support the petition by a reasoned statement, and it is our sincere hope, therefore, that in the interest of law and order you will accept the deputation from the Jewish People’s Council. The deputation will be led by James Hall, M.P. for Whitechapel and St. Georges, supported by A. M. Wall, Secretary of the London Trades Council, Father J. Groser of Christ Church, Watney Street, Stepney, E.1. and representatives of the Jewish People’s Council. Yours faithfully, J. Pearce Organising Secretary. Jewish People’s Council letter appealing for a meeting with Home Secretary Sir John Simon. Catalogue reference: HO 144/21060 Different publications took radically different positions in the days leading up to the march. The Jewish Chronicle issued a warning on the Saturday before the march urging Jewish people to keep away and going as far as to state: Jews who, however innocently, become involved in any possible disorders will be actively helping anti-Semitism and Jew-baiting. The Jewish Chronicle 'They shall not pass' The march went ahead with Sir Phillip Game, the Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, leading the policing of the event. The initial route was meant to see marchers’ parade down Commercial Street towards the East End. This was prevented by a huge crowd of anti-fascist demonstrators who blocked the intersection of Whitechapel High Street and Leman Street. A report in the Illustrated London News suggested a crowd of 100,000 counterdemonstrators was present. Although figures published at the time are now contested, they were significant and strongly outnumbers the fascists. Due to this the police advised a new route via Cable Street towards Stepney. On the new route, marchers continued to face pushback. On Cable Street, counterdemonstrators had overturned a brick-carrying truck to create a barricade. At the same time, they used the rallying cry ‘¡No pasarán!’ (meaning ‘they shall not pass’), which was commonly used by Spanish Republicans during this period. Stones and insults were also hurled, and Irish immigrant dockers who lived on the street joined in to stop the march moving forward. Following conversations between Game and Mosley, the fascists agreed to abandon the planned route and turned west towards the Embankment. Demonstrators at the junction of Aldgate and Commercial Road, from the Illustrated London News, 1936. Contrary to popular belief, much of the direct confrontation was not between the marchers and counterdemonstrators, but between the counterdemonstrators and the police. Children rolled marbles to make police horses fall over, and stones and insults were thrown towards the line of police officers trying to keep the two sides separated. This can be seen in an anonymised list of arrests which shows that of the 85 people arrested only six were fascists. The most common charges were insulting words and behaviour and obstructing police. A few were charged with the more serious crimes of grievous bodily harm and wilful damage. Interestingly, among the arrests were eight women and two children. The Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, Sir Phillip Game’s, account of the Battle of Cable Street Image 1 of 2 Page one of Sir Phillip Game’s account of the Battle of Cable Street. In this report, Game reports that he told Mosley, 'I am convinced that if you carry out your march and hold your meetings serious disorder is certain. I have therefore decided that neither the march nor the meetings can be allowed.' Catalogue reference: HO 144/21061 Image 2 of 2 Page two of Sir Phillip Game’s account of the Battle of Cable Street, including details on arrests. Catalogue reference: HO 144/21061 Previous Next Image 1 of 2 Image 2 of 2 The aftermath of Cable Street Despite the iconic status of these demonstrations as a triumph over fascism, in the wake of Cable Street the BUF’s membership increased. A report on the BUF notes that, by 27 October 1936, membership had increased by a little over 2,000. Most of these new members were from East End branches. Following the march and the violence of Cable Street, politicians and officials looked at ways to reduce the likelihood of similar events taking place again. The Public Order Bill was quickly developed, coming into law as The Public Order Act, in the beginning of January 1937. Among other things, the Act restricted the use of stewards at open air meetings and ensured that police had the power to ban marches or alter routes. It also outlawed the wearing of political uniforms. Among the banned uniforms were the black shirts of the British Union of Fascists. The BUF did not publicly disagree with the ruling, reiterating their ‘desire at all times to conform with the law of the land’ (catalogue reference: MEPO 3/2513). They did argue, however, that the police would not be able to ban the wearing of ‘an ordinary shirt of black colour with a black tie under an ordinary suit’. Open transcript British Union of Fascists and National Socialists Sanctuary Buildings, Great Smith Street, Westminster, S.W.1. 1 January, 1937. Sir, I thank you for your letter of the 31st December, and note that you are "not prepared to express an opinion" on the wearing of an ordinary shirt of black colour with a tie under an ordinary suit. I further note your statement that a Blackshirt is a "garment which has for some time past symbolised association with a political organisation" and beg to point out that the word employed in the Act is not "garment" but "uniform" and that on the legal interpretation of the latter word the whole issue rests. Pursuant to the advice in your letter of the 24th December we advised our members to discontinue wearing the Blackshirt uniform. Before advising them to adopt any distinctive mark which might show adherence to our Organisation we sought your opinion upon the legality of wearing an ordinary shirt of black colour with a tie under an ordinary suit. We need not remind you that such shirts can be bought in any shop, and have been worn for long past by some members of the public in no way associated with this organisation. We sought your opinion in order to prevent what might prove to be a widespread infringement of the law should the Courts later hold that such a shirt was in fact a uniform and, therefore, illegal. The fact that you did not see your way to give an opinion made it necessary for us to transmit our Counsel's advice to our members and leaves the responsibility for any infringement of the law upon the Home Office. Yours faithfully, N. Francis-Hawkins Director General of Organisation To: Commissioner of Police, New Scotland Yard, S.W.1. Letter from the British Union of Fascists regarding black shirts. Catalogue reference: MEPO 3/2513 Archives and collective memory The Battle of Cable Street signifies an important point in inter-war British history, when far-right political extremism was confronted on the streets of East London. While some claim that the immediate success of the coalition of anti-fascists has been overstated, memories of the event carry their own importance. The archival evidence allows us to re-engage with historical events and investigate their nuances. However, it is local community action and activity that decides how those events are remembered. Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection Focus on 'The first humble beginnings of an agitation': The 1866 mass women’s suffrage petition The 1866 mass women’s suffrage petition was an unprecedented moment in British history. Over 1,500 women were directly demanding the vote. What role did this petition play in making women’s suffrage a question of national significance? Author Vicky Iglikowski-Broad Roles Author Researcher Diverse Histories Records Specialist On this page The making of a movement The Kensington Society The organisers and their petition The signatories From petition to Parliament Legacy The making of a movement On 7 June 1866, a rolled parchment with 1,499 women’s signatures was delivered to Parliament. Although a few vital women’s petitions predated it, this was the first mass-scale women’s suffrage petition in Britain. The petition countered the persistent argument that women did not want the right to vote. Movements towards women’s suffrage, the right to vote, had begun to grow. Women had in practice long been excluded from formal parliamentary participation, but the Representation of the People Act 1832, also known as the Reform Act, legally prevented women from voting. It extended voting rights to more men but also defined voters as male. Suffrage organisations later referenced this time – and women’s exclusion in the Reform Act – as the start of their movement. The Act became a turning point, driving a campaign for change. The Reform Act 1832, Parliament’s archive collections. Catalogue reference: YHL/PO/PU/1/1832/2&3W4n147 Alongside the feminist reaction to the Reform Act, a movement for women’s rights was starting to grow across many fields, from education to domestic life, and legal reform. At the time, married women had no independent property rights. Divorce laws heavily favoured men. Women were barred from earning university degrees, and most professions remained closed to them. Class, as well as gender, shaped women’s experiences, with the impact often felt most sharply by working-class women. In 1854 artist and key women’s right campaigner Barbara Leigh Smith (later Bodichon), wrote the pamphlet A Brief Summary in Plain Language of the Most Important Laws of England Concerning Women. It exposed the reality of the inequalities women faced. A booklet called A brief review of the Women's Suffrage Movement since its beginnings in 1832. From the pamphlet collections of James Ramsay MacDonald, 1911. Catalogue reference: PRO 30/69/1834 The Kensington Society In March 1865, the Kensington Society was formed, named after the location of its meetings. Sharing members with the earlier women's club the Langham Place Group, this was a discussion society that brought together women who were eager for change. They debated progressive issues of the day, from education to working life. Notable figures included feminist Charlotte Manning as president, physician Sophia Jex-Blake , and educational reformer Elizabeth Wolstenholme Elmy. Votes for women was high on the society’s agenda, with philosopher and politician John Stuart Mill having recently included it in his election address as MP for Westminster in 1865. Giving women the vote became the topic for their second meeting, with a range of perspectives shared and broad backing. The Kensington Society offered a supportive feminist space, from which the 1866 petition was born. Photograph of a portrait of John Stuart Mill, painted by G F Watts, 1896. Catalogue reference: COPY 1/425/360 The organisers and their petition In May 1866, leading member Bodichon wrote to Helen Taylor, stepdaughter of Mill, about action 'towards getting women votes', suggesting a petition. Taylor thought it was 'highly desirable now'. While she felt no immediate results were likely to follow, she wrote: I think the most important thing is to make a demand and commence the first humble beginnings of an agitation… Helen Taylor, 9 May 1866. The Women's Library at the London School of Economics, reference: 7BMC/B Petitions were one of the few parliamentary tools available to women at this time. Their action followed in the tradition of abolitionists (the movement to end the trade in enslaved peoples) and Chartists (who pushed for democratic reform in 19th century). There’s a palpable excitement in the organisers letters as they start to plan their action. The related correspondence is available to view at The Women’s Library at the London School of Economics (LSE), as well as a printed copy of the petition. Kensington Society members Bodichon, Taylor, Emily Davies, and Elizabeth Garrett became the key organisers of the petition. At the same time Garrett was challenging the University of London’s refusal to grant exam certificates to women (which did not change until 1878) – just one example of their work across campaigns. Strategically seizing the opportunity presented by a newly proposed Reform Bill, together the women drafted a concise, legally framed petition focused on civic duties, taxation, and representation – deliberately avoiding divisive debates about which women should be eligible to vote. As was usual, the petition in its original form does not survive but a copy of the text is recorded in the Committee on Public Petitions. Open transcript Public petitions – appendix to the twenty-seventh report. Delivered June 13th. Containing Petitions presented June 6-8, 1866. Elective Franchise (for Extension to all Householders without Distinction of Sex). Metropolis. App. 747. Mr. John Stuart Mill. Sig. 1521. 8501. The humble Petition of the Undersigned, Sheweth, That it having been expressly laid down by high authorities that the possession of property in this country carries with it the right to vote in the election of representatives in Parliament, it is an evident anomaly that some holders of property are allowed to use this right, while others, forming no less a constituent part of the nation, and equally qualified by law to hold property, are not able to exercise this privilege. That the participation of women in the Government is consistent with the principles of the British Constitution, inasmuch as women in these islands have always been held capable of sovereignty, and women are eligible for various public offices. Your Petitioners therefore humbly pray your honorable House to consider the expediency of providing for the representation of all householders, without distinction of sex, who possess such property or rental qualification as your honorable House may determine. And your Petitioners will ever pray. BARBARA L. S. BODICHON. MENTIA TAYLOR. EMILY DAVIES. &c. &c. &c. Copy of the 1866 mass suffrage petition text, from the Appendix to Reports of the Committee on Public Petitions, 1866, Parliament’s archive collections. Catalogue reference: YHC/CL/JO/6/417 Collecting the signatures was done in just a few weeks. This was a remarkable logistical feat, something that is hard to imagine in our time of online petitions and mobile phones. Signatures were mainly collated by post and physically assembled at the home of radical MP Peter Taylor and activist Mentia Taylor, Aubrey House in London. Open transcript Aubrey House, Aubrey Road, Kensington Name and Surname of each Person Peter Alfred Taylor Age of Male/Female Male, 41 Relation to Head of Family Head Rank, Profession, or Occupation Crepe Manufacturer Where born St Pancras, Middlesex Name and Surname of each Person Clementia Taylor Age of Male/Female Female, 49 Relation to Head of Family Wife Rank, Profession, or Occupation - Where born Brockdish, Norfolk 1861 census schedule for Aubrey house, Kensington, home of Clementia and Peter Alfred Taylor. Catalogue reference: RG 9/14/333 The signatories The signatories came from every corner of the UK and Ireland, from Leeds to St Andrews, and even included British women living abroad. Organisers mobilised contacts built through years of campaigning, family, friends and local networks. While the instigators were mainly educated middle-class and upper-class women, the signatories themselves included shopkeepers, domestic workers and laundresses. Prominent campaigners signed the petition, such as Frances Power Cobbe, who led campaigns for divorce reform. Similarly, signatories Jessie Boucherett, Sarah Lewin, and Gertrude J King were all politically active and on the committee of the Society for Promoting the Employment of Women. This aimed to offer women training to move into the professions and be more financially independent. Photograph of petition signatory and organiser Miss Frances Power Cobbe, 1896. Catalogue reference: COPY 1/425/300 Sarah Parker Remond , an abolitionist and feminist, who was born in America and described herself as 'of African descent', signed while living at Aubrey House in London, where the petition was organised. Today, Ann Dingsdale’s pioneering research shows female-headed households were more likely to sign, such as shopkeepers Barbara Loftus and her daughter who sold baby clothes. Another was the Miall sisters. They collectively ran a girls’ school in Broughton and all three signed the petition. They wanted the girls they were educating to have a say in shaping society. The diversity of signatories challenges the stereotype that early feminism was exclusive to elite or metropolitan women, revealing a broader-based, intergenerational section of women interested in reform. Open transcript To the Right Honourable Sir George Grey, Baronet, Her Majesty’s Principal Secretary of State for the Home Department. The Memorial of Sarah Parker Remond of Aubrey House, Notting Hill in the County of Middlesex. Sheweth That your Memorialist is desirous of obtaining for herself a Certificate of Naturalisation pursuant to the Act of Parliament passed in the eighth year of the Reign of Her present Majesty entitled “Act to amend the Law relating to Aliens” That your memorialist is of African descent and a native of Salem, Massachusetts in the United States of America. That your Memorialist is forty-one years of age and is unmarried. That your Memorialist’s settled place of residence is in London. That your Memorialist has resided uninterruptedly in the Country for the last six years and upwards and it is her intention to continue to reside permanently within the United Kingdom. That the Grounds upon which your Memorialist seeks to obtain the rights and capacities of a natural born British subject are as British citizenship application from abolitionist and physician Sarah Parker Remond , the only known Black woman to sign the petition. Catalogue reference: HO 1/123/4809 The strategic organisers planned to print and share copies with the press and MPs. This meant signing a public statement. It was not an easy decision, with some fearing for their reputation or impacts on other campaign work. Dorothea Beale, suffragist and Principal of Cheltenham Ladies’ College, was a Kensington Society member who declined to sign the petition, fearing it might affect her educational work. She later founded St Hilda’s College, Oxford. Approximately half of Kensington Society members signed the petition, but many did not. From petition to Parliament Taylor noted that anything more than 100 signatures would be 'very satisfactory'. In the end the printed petition had 1,499 names. Last-minute additions brought the official count to 1,521 on the version handed to Parliament. Open transcript 11 am Monday. Dear Miss Taylor We are getting on towards 700 names — is it not capital! [capital - common expression of enthusiasm at the time] I saw Mr Russell Gurney at 9 am. The ladies all want him to present the petition & he says he will if Mr Mill wishes it & will speak to Mr Mill to-day. Letter from Barbara Bodichon to Helen Taylor updating her excitedly on the number of signatures received. The Women's Library at the London School of Economics, reference: 7BMC On the day of delivery, Garrett and Davies carried the roll through Parliament – an unfamiliar experience to them given the male dominated nature of politics. The petition roll was physically large to handle, and legend goes that Garett and Davies concealed it behind an apple cart stall; a moment memorialised by the movement. On receiving the petition Mill remarked, ‘I can brandish this with effect!’ and presented it to the House of Commons. Although the petition brought no immediate change it marked a turning point, making women’s suffrage a formal parliamentary issue for the first time. The petition was quickly followed by Mill’s landmark 1867 speech and vote on women’s suffrage, which argued for legislation to use the word 'person'. The first women’s suffrage bill followed in 1870, introduced by Jacob Bright MP, a key parliamentary supporter whose sister Priscilla signed the 1866 petition. From this point on debates on women's suffrage took place almost every year in Parliament. Open transcript 1866. The first Petition was presented to the House of Commons by Mr. John Stuart Mill, signed by 1500 women. 1867. May 4. Mr. Mill moved his amendment to the Representation of the People Bill “to leave out man and substitute person”. Lost by 196 to 83. 1870. Mr. Jacob Bright introduced a Bill to remove the electoral disabilities of women. 2nd Reading carried 124—91. Committee stage defeated 94—220. Internal Home Office document on the 'History of the Female Suffrage question in Parliament', written during an attempt to pass suffrage legislation in 1888. Catalogue reference: HO 45/9785/B2940 Petitioning became a core campaigning method, used strategically alongside other tactics. In 1873, Lady Anna Gore-Langton, a suffragist and signatory to the petition, used political lobbying as another approach. She warned Viscount Chelsea Cadogan that 'several ladies will work to prevent his election in Bath' if he opposed women’s suffrage. Campaigners also worked on multiple fronts, with the vote being just one focus. In 1870, the Married Women’s Property Act passed after decades of campaigning, granting married women the right to own property and keep earnings. Suffrage petition organiser Bodichon was a key figure in both campaigns. These women also got involved in other mechanisms for influencing society, where available to them, such as being elected to London School Boards. Open transcript May 8th / 73 [Printed letterhead] NEWTON PARK, BRISTOL. Dear Lord Chelsea, Pray pardon me for troubling you by writing on the question of the political enfranchisement of Women who are householders & rate payers. My apology is that I am President of the Woman’s Committee in Bath. I was sorry to hear from Mrs Pea[ch], that your opinions are supposed to be unfavourable to this question. I do hope// [next page] that is a mistake, that you have not made up your mind that you cannot support this bill. Lady Anna Gore-Langton, Newton Park, Bristol, to Viscount Chelsea Cadogan, 8 Feb 1873, Parliament’s archive collections. Catalogue reference: YCAD/132 Legacy Despite later divisions, many suffrage organisations could trace their origins back to the early petition committee; the post-petition momentum spurred the formation of suffrage societies in Manchester, Edinburgh, and London. In 1890, a 'Survivors' Petition', signed by 78 original petitioners including Bodichon and Garrett Anderson, was presented to Parliament. It highlighted that the situation for women had not changed since the original petition. Over decades of persistent campaigning, petitioning remained central to the movement, alongside legal challenges, meetings, deputations, and eventually militant protest. Many original petitioners remained active. Taylor attempted to circumvent the law by standing for parliamentary election in 1885, and later focused on socialism and Irish land reform. In 1869 Davies co-founded Girton College, the first women's college at Cambridge. Garrett Anderson became England’s first woman mayor in 1908. Others, like Millicent Fawcett, who was too young to sign but witnessed her sister Garrett's involvement, were inspired by the petition and went on to lead major suffrage organisations. Dame Millicent Garrett Fawcett, oil painting, by Annie L. Swynnerton, 1910. Photo Courtesy: UK Parliament, WOA 7739 heritagecollections.parliament.uk Some women gained the vote in 1918, and full franchise equality came in 1928 over 60 years after the petition. Few original signatories lived to see it, though Emily Davies cast her vote aged 88 in 1918. The petition gave women a collective voice, showing what was possible when they organised and acted together. As Helen Taylor reflected at the time of the petition: It is indeed a wonderful success. It does honour the energy of those who have worked in it and promises well for the prospects of any future plan for furthering the same subjects. Helen Taylor, 8 June 1866. Catalogue reference: FD 7/2308 During its development, many considered in vitro fertilisation (IVF) unethical. Records at The National Archives highlight how this view has changed over time and brings to light the people who fought for, and against, its use. Author Dr Laura Robson-Mainwaring Roles Author Researcher Principal Records Specialist – Modern Health On this page Louise Brown: A glimmer of hope Filming the first IVF birth Developing IVF A new technology raises new questions Voices from the public: Fear and hope A new world The legacy of IVF Louise Brown: A glimmer of hope In July 1978, the world witnessed a medical milestone: the birth of Louise Brown, the first baby conceived through in vitro fertilisation (IVF). The technique, developed by Patrick Steptoe, Robert Edwards, and Jean Purdy, involves fertilising an egg outside the body before transferring the embryo to the uterus. The success of this process marked the beginning of a scientific and social transformation. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, well before Louise’s birth, the press began sharing concerns about IVF. UK Government records, held by The National Archives, show that this publicity alarmed the public and many people were concerned about the ethical implications of IVF. For couples experiencing infertility, however, these medical developments created hope and presented a potential path to parenthood. Image 1 of 2 Newspaper clipping from The Guardian for an article titled 'Time ripe for first tube baby', 4 January 1972. Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 Image 2 of 2 Newspaper clipping from the Daily Sketch for an article titled 'Doctor in plea for test tube baby inquiry', 2 November 1970. Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 Previous Next Image 1 of 2 Image 2 of 2 From our collection MH 166/928 Title Government consultation, correspondence and minutes of meetings regarding IVF Date 1965–1973 At this time, advances in reproductive medicine, IVF, surrogacy, and later gene editing, created profound ethical questions such as: When does human life begin? Is it acceptable to manipulate embryos? Who holds parental rights? How should society guard against exploitation and unequal access? Today, IVF is a well-accepted part of reproductive healthcare. In 2023 alone, one in every 32 births in the UK were the result of IVF treatment, which is equivalent to one child in every classroom. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, however, the technology was unprecedented and considered controversial. Filming the first IVF birth A file (catalogue reference: INF 12/13/1399) from the Central Office of Information (COI) shows the widespread public interest surrounding Louise Brown’s birth. Ministers decided to commission the COI to produce an official film. This footage would assess the baby’s condition at birth and create a historical record of IVF’s use. Lesley Brown (Louise’s mother) also decided to sell her story exclusively to Associated Newspapers Ltd (Daily Mail) before entering Oldham General District Hospital. This meant, frustratingly for the Department of Health and Social Security (DHSS), that there would be a 28–day embargo (waiting period) before any footage they recorded could be shared publicly. On Monday 24 July, the DHSS asked the COI’s Films Division to be ready to film the birth of the world’s first IVF baby. Our records show that, throughout the day, COI stayed in touch with the Regional Health Authority and Steptoe, who confirmed that the birth would not happen before Thursday evening. On that basis, the film crew was told to stand down for 24 hours, but everything changed the next morning. At 11:30 am on Tuesday 25 July, Tony Buckingham from the Regional Health Authority phoned with an urgent warning that the birth could happen at any moment. As a result, the COI sent the film crew racing to Oldham. Final filming rights were secured, including from Mrs Brown at 11:15 pm. Just 15 minutes later at 11:30 pm, the caesarean section began. Louise was born at 11:47 pm, weighing 5 lbs 12 oz. The footage is preserved at the British Film Institute (BFI) and made available online by Wellcome Collection. Open transcript TEST TUBE BABY 24 MINUTE NEWS ITEM At 23.47 BST on 25 July 1978 a unique baby was born in Britain - the result of a "test-tube" fertilisation. Louise Joy Brown, the 51b 12oz daughter of Mr and Mrs Brown of Bristol, was delivered safely by Caesarian section by Patrick Steptoe Esq FRCS FRCOG, Honarary Consultant Gynaecologist at the Oldham General Hospital near Manchester. He was assisted by Dr John Webster MB ChB MRCOG, by Dr Finlay Campbell FSARCS DA (Anaesthetist), Theatre Sister Astel SRN and Sister Marshall SRN, Dr. Hilson MAMB BChir FRCP(L) FRCP(E) MRCS DCH (Consultant Paediatrician). Also present at the birth was Dr Robert Edwards DSc PhD, the Cambridge physiologist whose 20 years of research led to the successful fertilisation. The historic birth was commented on by Dr Edwards as "A close collaboration between scientist and doctor". Length: 86 1/2 ft 26.33 metres Time: 2 mins 24 secs at 24 fps 2 mins 17 secs at 25 fps Sales enquiries please to: Sales Unit Film and Television Division Central Office of Information Hercules Road London SEl Tel. 01-928 2345, Ext 227 or 224 Telex 91544 CENTROFORM LDN Memorandum showing the description of the two minute news reel produced by the COI at the birth of Louise Brown, 1978. There was a longer (15 minute) clinical version , narrated by Steptoe. Please note, both videos contain graphic depictions of a medical procedure (a cesarean section). Catalogue reference: INF 12/1399 From our collection INF 12/1399 Title Central Office of Information's notes on their film coverage of the birth of the first 'test tube' baby Date July–October 1978 Developing IVF In the early 1970s, Edwards and Steptoe were developing techniques that would eventually lead to Louise’s birth. Records of the Medical Research Council (MRC) show that they applied for funding in May 1971 but were turned down on ethical grounds. For most of the 1970s, the MRC viewed IVF as too experimental, too risky, and too poorly supported by clinical infrastructure to justify funding . The MRC instead encouraged them to undertake studies on animals. Open transcript 2. Long-term support declined (a) Dr R.G. Edwards (University of Cambridge) and Mr P.C. Steptoe (consultant gynaecologist, Oldham): application for long-term support for studies on human reproduction (MRC 71/239). The application was declined because of serious doubts about the ethical aspects of the proposed investigations, especially those relating to the implantation in women of oocytes fertilized in vitro which were considered premature. Dr Edwards should, however, be encouraged, without commitment, to undertake studies of the type proposed in animals. Medical Research Council Meeting ‘Long-term support denied’, 20 May 1971, Catalogue reference: FD 13/171 From our collection FD 13/171 Title Notes from the Medical Research Council's Meeting Date May 1971 Despite the rejection, their research continued with private funding. After the safe and successful birth of the first IVF baby, Louise, the MRC became a strong supporter of IVF research. This opened the door to mainstream clinical development and a state-focused examination of the ethical issues involved. A new technology raises new questions The Committee of Inquiry into Human Fertilisation and Embryology, chaired by the moral philosopher Dame Mary Warnock, was established in 1982 by the DHSS. Its members included doctors, scientists, a psychologist, and faith representatives, reflecting the scientific, social, and moral issues at stake. Together, they discussed whether IVF should be permitted, and if so, how it should be regulated. They also discussed the moral status of an embryo created in a laboratory and whether the state should regulate who could access IVF. The fundamental moral objection to IVF was that, for the procedure to be successful, several eggs must be fertilised, meaning that some embryos are likely to be destroyed or discarded during the process. This is because not all embryos develop successfully, so multiple embryos are created to increase the chances of a successful pregnancy. Despite this, their final report approved the use of IVF, with some limitations, and recommended the creation of a voluntary licensing authority, an independent body that would monitor IVF clinics to ensure ethical standards were being followed. It also concluded that commercial surrogacy was unethical, meaning the carrier of an embryo cannot be paid by the parent(s) for carrying their baby. Additionally, the committee suggested that human embryos used in research should not be kept alive in vitro beyond 14 days as this would be unethical. Although the report was signed by all members, differing views on when life begins led to expressions of dissent within the report that, they claimed, ‘ reflected the range of views in society ’. The report went on to lay the basis for the regulatory framework established by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990. Open transcript MRC/RCOG Voluntary Licensing Authority for Human In Vitro Fertilisation and Embryology. Guidelines for both clinical and research applications of Human In Vitro Fertilisation 1985. The Voluntary Licensing Authority (VLA) is jointly sponsored by the Medical Research Council and the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists. Guidelines for clinical and research applications for Human In Vitro Fertilisation from the voluntary licensing authority,1985. Catalogue reference: FD 7/3321 From our collection FD 7/3321 Title Reports, notes and correspondence on IVF Date 1986–1989 Voices from the public: Fear and hope Letters from ordinary people, found in the archive, capture the emotional and moral intensity of the public debate around IVF. One correspondent wrote, 'Research babies in bottles’, I’ve never heard of anything so repulsive. Letter from a member of the public to the Secretary of State for Social Services, 2 November 1970., Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 We heartily disapprove of this research, because if nature decides that children should not be born then artificial means should not be used. Imagine a child having to realise he was a test tube child. Letter from a member of the public to the Lord President of the Council, 30 January 1974., Catalogue reference: INF 12/1399 Open transcript February 26th 1967. The Minister of Health Dear Sir In view of the clear admission on ITN news this evening that experiments on human foetuses will be a necessary preliminary to the successful implantation in the womb of eggs fertilised outside the human body, would you kindly give me an answer to the following points: a) do yon personally approve of this technique in making childbirth possible? b) Do you personally consider that there are no ethical objections to the experimentation currently in progress? c) Are National Health and/or University facilities being used for this research? d) Have you power to direct that such experiments cease? e) If so, will you provide the direction the medical profession is seeking, and order an immediate cessation of these activities? You can no doubt deduce my own attitude. Yours sincerely John Wilson (Liberal Prospective Parliamentary Candidate for Hemel Hempstead) Letter from Parliamentary Candidate John Wilson to the Minister of Health, 26 February 1967. Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 Others wrote pleading for access to treatment, revealing the emotional toll of infertility and the personal stakes behind the debates. One couple who had been married for ten years described themselves as living ‘in a hopeless condition’ and asked to ‘participate in this service to humanity… We are willing to accept your terms of payment (whatever it may be).’ Open transcript 12th May ‘73 The Ministry of Health, London Re: Test Tube Babies Sir Recently in one of our local papers we came across one article which has inspired us to write this letter. We are a sterile couple, married for the last ten years: in the 7th year of our married life my Mrs had to undergo an emergency operation. Right phallopean [sic] tube bursted [sic] due to advanced ectopic pregnancy (approx. 2 ½ months). While cutting and clamping the doctors thought it wise to remove cyst from left tube also, however unfortunately the second tube along with cyst was removed, leaving us completely incapable to conceive & in hopeless condition. We accepted the life as if we have lost a limb & are living the life of satisfaction. However when we read the report in the paper that in U.K. you are successful in planting fertilised ovum in the womb and baby could develop thereafter. We have thought it wise to refer this matter to you and we wonder whether we could participate in this service to humanity & be benefited with your success. We are willing to accept your terms of payment etc (whatever it may be). It will be in order to mention here that we are a couple of 35/33 yrs of age (husb/wife) physically fit. Sperm count: 120 million/cc & all other qualities/quantities being above normal: m.c. regular. If you require any certificate or any medical opinion/ questioning to be answered we will be too glad to furnish the same. We hope you will extend you helping hand before we get too old to participate. Sincerely thanking you [signature]. A letter from a couple dealing with fertility challenges to the Ministry of Health, 12 May 1973. Catalogue reference: MH 156/458 Patients of Patrick Steptoe also wrote in his defence. After spotting a local newspaper report in Oldham’s Evening Chronicle suggesting his work was a step toward euthanasia, one woman passionately directed her letter to Prime Minister James Callaghan: Mr Steptoe is my doctor, and I am involved in these ‘experiments’ as they put it…. I have met so many young women in Dr Kershaws Hospital whilst we have been receiving treatment, we all love Mr Steptoe very much indeed, he is our only hope to have a child of our own, he is a kind, considerate and very wonderful man, and all he is trying to do is help us, we have no other hope, at all… It’s a terrible thing to be told you can’t have a child, and then all of a sudden you meet Mr Steptoe and there’s a glimmer of hope. A patient of Dr Steptoe to the Prime Minister James Callaghan, undated letter., Catalogue reference MH 156/458 Open transcript …that a Mr. A Mcgarty was going to ask you to investigate Mr Steptoe’s work, this is why I’m writing to you put ‘our’ side of the story to you as well. I say ‘our’ because I have met so many young women in the Kershaw’s Hospital whilst we have been receiving treatment, we all love Mr Steptoe very much indeed, he is our only hope to have a child of our own, he is a kind, considerate man, and all he is trying to do is help us, we have no other hope, at all. Please, ask your wife her feelings, as a women, I’m sure she’ll understand, it’s a terrible thing to be told you can’t have… Page from multi-page letter from a patient of Dr Steptoe to the Prime Minister James Callaghan, undated letter. Catalogue reference MH 156/458 From our collection MH 156/458 Title Background documents and correspondence on IVF and the birth of Louise Brown Date 1973–1979 Another patient of Steptoe, describing the treatment as her only hope, wrote: If the people objecting to this treatment had experiences the torment and misery of a woman who is unable to conceive I am sure they would look at this matter in a different light. Letter from a patient of Dr Steptoe to her local MP, 22 May 1969., Catalogue reference: FD 9/1430 From our collection FD 9/1430 Title Enquiries from the public on IVF research Date 1969–1973 A new world Following the successful birth of Louise Brown, Steptoe, Edwards and Purdy worked towards founding Bourn Hall, which became the world’s first IVF clinic in 1980. Here, they worked to advance IVF techniques. Around this time, advancements were also happening across the globe, with the world’s second IVF baby being born in October 1978 in Kolkata, India. Image 1 of 2 Extracts of a leaflet for Bourn Hall IVF Clinic, 1985. Catalogue reference: FD 7/3334 Image 2 of 2 The leaflet reads, 'Collecting these samples will be organised by the nursing staff. The results of the hormone investigations will enable the time of ovulation to be accurately predicted. (b) When ovulation is imminent, the wife will be notified that the egg recovery procedure will shortly take place, and she will be prepared for the operation, which is again a laparoscopy technique. Based on the Clinic's work to date, the percentage of eggs recovered is very high. (c) When the time of ovulation is diagnosed, the husband will be asked to attend the Clinic to provide a fresh semen sample, for fertilisation of his wife's egg. The process of fertilisation is carried out in an exceptionally sterile environment and the embryology work of nurturing the embryo to the stage where replacement can be effected takes approximately 3 days. The percentage of eggs successfully fertilised is over 80%. (d) Replacement of the fertilised egg (embryo) will be carried out in the operating theatre, usually without anaesthesia. (e) A period of a few hours rest and medical care will then follow, until the wife is advised she can leave. ... Previous Next Image 1 of 2 Image 2 of 2 From our collection FD 7/2308 Title Files from the inquiry into Human Fertilisation and Embryology (Warnock Committee). Date 1982–1984 From our collection FD 7/3334 Title Files related to Bourn Hall Clinic, Cambridge. Date 1985–1989 Sadly, Jean Purdy passed away in 1985 after helping to develop and refine the laboratory techniques that made IVF possible. Patrick Steptoe died in 1988, having helped transform fertility treatment through his pioneering work in laparoscopy and IVF alongside Edwards. Their contributions established IVF as a viable medical option for overcoming infertility and offered hope to millions of couples worldwide. Following Steptoe's death, Dame Mary Donaldson, Chair of the Voluntary Licensing Authority, described him as: ... a man of pioneering spirit but also one of great integrity. His death marks the end of an era but his influence will undoubtedly spread into the next. Dame Mary Donaldson to Mrs P Steptoe, 23 March 1988, Catalogue reference: FD 7/3334 Bourn Hall Clinic still operates today, and Steptoe, Edwards, and Purdy’s work continues to have a global impact. The legacy of IVF The archival material surrounding the development of IVF is invaluable for understanding how governments and society responded to the challenges posed by new reproductive technologies. While IVF is not a definitive cure for infertility and does not always succeed, it continues to offer hope to many. This was made possible by the pioneering work of figures such as Steptoe, Edwards, and Purdy, as well as the persistent hope of the hundreds of women involved in their early experiments. nhs.uk Would you like to learn more about IVF?
